prompt: Governments have limited budgets for health care. Some people believe that public money should always be spent on preventing illness rather than on treating it. To what extent do you agree or disagree?
essay:
Prevention is cheaper. Almost nobody disputes it, which makes it worth asking why health ministers who announce prevention programmes go on funding hospitals. I agree that spending should tilt much further towards prevention than it currently does. I disagree with 'always', because the reason prevention keeps losing these arguments is not ignorance, and a policy built on the assumption that it is will lose them too.

The economics are not in doubt. A vaccination programme, a screening service or a serious effort to reduce smoking costs a small fraction of the treatment it displaces, and the saving compounds across a lifetime rather than arriving once. Prevention also reaches people before the point at which their illness becomes both expensive and difficult, which is the point at which a treatment-only system first hears from them at all.

What defeats it is that its beneficiaries cannot be named. Screening saves lives without anyone knowing whose; the person who did not develop the disease never learns that they were about to. Treatment, by contrast, always has a face, a ward and a family, and when a minister is asked to justify a decision it is that face which appears in the newspaper. This is not irrationality on the public's part. A society that could be argued out of treating the identifiably ill in favour of a statistical benefit would be a worse society rather than a more efficient one, and the instinct protecting them is worth keeping.

So the honest position is a strong tilt rather than an absolute. Guarantee treatment to those already ill, and route the growth in the budget towards prevention, where the marginal money does more good. The shift then happens without anybody being asked to sacrifice a named patient to an averaged one, which is the only version of this argument that has ever survived contact with a real health service.
title: Whether prevention should always come before treatment
